candidate_claims.why_load_bearing: If the working assumption in defense trade press is that small AI/autonomous drones fail in Arctic cold, that steers Army/Air Force procurement at JBER and Eielson away from the entire small-UAS class toward expensive large platforms, and shapes which firms win Alaska-specific autonomy contracts and how 11th Airborne readiness is judged.

prelim_counter_evidence.fact: The same Breaking Defense article reports the Vector AI drone from Quantum Systems 'can fly for up to three hours in negative 20 to 30 degrees' - directly within the range where other drones failed, indicating the constraint is battery/materials engineering and acquisition choice, not a categorical Arctic impossibility for AI drones.

candidate_claims.recurrence_note: Amplified by The Defense Post (Jan 27 2026) and Army Recognition (2025-2026) from the 11th Airborne's Alaska exercises; active recurring readiness frame for Arctic operations.

candidate_claims.claim_verbatim: We put downward pressure on the rates for everyone on that system
candidate_claims.claim_paraphrase_fair: Siting AI/compute data centers at Alaskan hydro facilities benefits all ratepayers by reducing per-unit electricity costs for the entire community.
candidate_claims.why_load_bearing: Enoka's rate-reduction claim is the central community-benefit argument used to justify siting AI data centers at rural Alaskan utilities; co-op boards in Petersburg, Wrangell, Ketchikan are evaluating Greensparc proposals on this rationale. If the benefit is conditional or not replicable, those permitting decisions rest on false premises.

prelim_counter_evidence.fact: Petersburg Municipal Power and Light Director Karl Hagerman: 'It is very rare that any utility that I've been involved with in Petersburg sees an opportunity to have downward pressure on rates' - implying the claim is conditional.
The Cordova pilot uses 170 kW of a facility where 20-25% of annual hydropower goes unused; most communities lack that spilled-energy profile.

candidate_claims.recurrence_note: Repeated at the Governor's Energy Conference (May 2026), CleanTechnica (Mar 2026), DOE/NLR Cordova feature; echoed by Clay Koplin (Cordova Electric CEO).

candidate_claims.claim_verbatim: GenAI has become essential for organizations because of its ability to accelerate problem-solving, increase productivity and aid decision-making while reducing the time employees spend on repetitive tasks which frees them up to focus on more strategic work
candidate_claims.claim_paraphrase_fair: Generative AI adoption has become a business necessity for Alaskan organizations, not an optional upgrade.
candidate_claims.why_load_bearing: Alaska Communications is a primary managed-services provider for enterprise and government clients statewide; Knipp's 'essential' framing drives procurement conversations with hospitals, state agencies, and resource companies. prelim_counter_evidence.fact: Woodrie Burich (AkBizMag 2026 leadership series) cited a Deloitte study finding 'only 5 percent of AI implementations are meeting expectations' and 'approximately 95 percent of organizations are getting zero return on AI projects.'
Same Burich piece: 'AI doesn't reduce work. It intensifies it by expanding scope, accelerating pace' and '57 percent of employees are already using it without leadership visibility.'

candidate_claims.recurrence_note: Press release carried by Business Wire, Yahoo Finance, Nasdaq, Fiber Broadband Association, The AI Journal, Barchart - 7+ outlets.

candidate_claims.claim_verbatim: The base requirement for tapping into AI is connectivity.
candidate_claims.claim_paraphrase_fair: Connectivity is the foundational prerequisite for Alaskans to benefit from AI, implying that solving connectivity solves Alaska's AI-access problem.
candidate_claims.why_load_bearing: Justifies the $629M BEAD deployment as an AI-access strategy. If connectivity alone is the binding constraint, completing the $1.02B Alaska BEAD allocation unlocks AI adoption; if device access, AI literacy, compute, and data sovereignty are equally binding, the framing misallocates.

prelim_counter_evidence.fact: Alaska has the fewest AI and data center jobs of any U.S. state at 119 (2025 BLS), indicating connectivity to date has not translated into AI workforce participation even in connected regions.

candidate_claims.recurrence_note: Mirrored in Murkowski/Sullivan BEAD releases linking funding to economic opportunity without disaggregating AI requirements. NOTE: risk of overlap with already-corrected 6/13 broadband-careers claim; treat as a distinct connectivity-as-sufficient angle only.

candidate_claims.why_load_bearing: The 'few jobs per megawatt' framing is the most widely reproduced objection to Alaska's data-center-as-economic-engine narrative, driving legislative skepticism and Anchorage Assembly zoning scrutiny. If the relevant metric is fiscal yield per megawatt rather than jobs per megawatt, a correction shifts the policy conversation.

prelim_counter_evidence.fact: The Stak Energy North Slope project's state preliminary approval cites 1,500 peak construction jobs and 60 permanent jobs for a $500M facility - low permanent count but comparable to oil-and-gas facilities Alaska already prizes.
Ethan Berkowitz (Far North Digital) projects $705M/year in state and local tax revenue from a single 1-GW campus, suggesting the metric is fiscal yield per MW, not jobs per MW.

candidate_claims.recurrence_note: Live and circulating 19 months across Alaska Beacon, Frontiersman, Homer News, Route Fifty; reappears in Roger Kaye (ADN Jan 3 2026) and Rep. McCabe (ADN Apr 1 2026). NOTE: data-center-economics angle, distinct from already-corrected power/gas/cooling claims.
